title: Ἐλάτη καὶ βάτος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 101. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἤριζον πρὸς ἀλλήλας ἐλάτη καὶ βάτος.
sentences.tr: Ērizon pros allēlas elatē kai batos.
sentences.l: A fir and a bramble were quarrelling with each other.
sentences.n: ἐλάτη is the silver fir, the tall straight timber of masts and roof-beams; βάτος is the bramble that sprawls at knee height. The two are chosen for the greatest possible distance between them.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἐλάτη ἑαυτὴν ἐπαινοῦσα ἔφη ὅτι « καλή εἰμι καὶ εὐμήκης καὶ ὑψηλὴ καὶ χρησιμεύω εἰς ναῶν στέγη καὶ εἰς πλοῖα· καὶ πῶς ἐμοὶ συγκρίνῃ ; »
sentences.tr: Hē de elatē heautēn epainousa ephē hoti « kalē eimi kai eumēkēs kai hypsēlē kai chrēsimeuō eis naōn stegē kai eis ploia· kai pōs emoi synkrinēi ; »
sentences.l: And the fir, praising herself, said that « I am fair and well-grown and lofty, and I am useful for the roofs of temples and for ships; and how do you compare yourself with me? »
sentences.i: And the fir, praising herself, said: « I am beautiful and tall and lofty, and I serve for temple roofs and for ships — how do you set yourself beside me? »
sentences.n: The recitative ὅτι again, followed by the fir's own first-person words: the Greek writes 'said that «I am…»' where English simply opens the quotation. στέγη here is the neuter plural of στέγος, 'roofs', not the feminine singular στέγη. συγκρίνῃ is second person singular, middle or passive in form, 'you measure yourself against, you are set beside'; the dative ἐμοί is the standard the comparison is made to.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ βάτος εἶπεν· « Εἰ μνησθῇς τῶν πελέκεων καὶ τῶν πριόνων τῶν σε κοπτόντων, βάτος γενέσθαι καὶ σὺ μᾶλλον θελήσεις. »
sentences.tr: Hē de batos eipen· « Ei mnēsthēis tōn pelekeōn kai tōn prionōn tōn se koptontōn, batos genesthai kai sy mallon thelēseis. »
sentences.l: And the bramble said: « If you call to mind the axes and the saws that cut you, you too will rather wish to become a bramble. »
sentences.n: μιμνήσκομαι takes the genitive of what is remembered, τῶν πελέκεων καὶ τῶν πριόνων. εἰ with the aorist subjunctive μνησθῇς stands where classical prose writes ἐάν; the apodosis is a plain future indicative, θελήσεις, so the condition looks forward as a real one, not a remote one. The bramble's argument is the useless plant's only argument, and it is unanswerable.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ἐν βίῳ ὄντας ἐπαίρεσθαι ἐν τῇ δόξῃ· τῶν γὰρ εὐτελῶν ἀκίνδυνός ἐστιν ὁ βίος.
sentences.tr: Hoti ou dei en biōi ontas epairesthai en tēi doxēi· tōn gar eutelōn akindynos estin ho bios.
sentences.l: That those who are in life must not be lifted up in their glory; for the life of those of no account is free from danger.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who are alive must not be puffed up with their glory; for the life of the lowly is free from danger.
sentences.n: A moral opening with a bare Ὅτι: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἐπαίρεσθαι is the passive of ἐπαίρω, 'to be raised up', and is the standing word for being elated by one's own importance. εὐτελής is literally 'costing little', and of persons 'of no account' — the bramble's own condition, praised.
